speaker: John
line: Imagine a graduate course called Scientific Agents and Materials Workflows. Today's lecture is on MatToolBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real-World Materials Science Workflows. As computer-use research expands, O-S-World 2.0 studies long-horizon desktop tasks, while ScienceBoard examines realistic scientific workflows. This paper, from researchers including Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Suzhou Laboratory, brings those directions together in specialized materials software. The field is moving toward agents that act across real applications; this work asks whether they can do so reliably in science. I see Noah's hand—go ahead, Noah.

speaker: Noah
line: Hi Professor, is the core idea simply to test whether an agent can click through scientific software?

speaker: John
line: That is part of it, but the benchmark tests more than clicking. It asks whether an agent can carry out a meaningful workflow while preserving the scientific state and producing usable outputs. The distinction matters: an interface action can look plausible yet select the wrong data, apply an unsuitable operation, or save an artifact that another tool cannot use. The benchmark measures operational competence, not whether an analysis is scientifically valid.

speaker: John
line: MatToolBench contains 204 tasks across ten tools, spanning graphical applications, scientific plotting, database access, and materials-analysis programming. The tasks use authentic files, including X-ray diffraction patterns, X-ray photoelectron spectra, microscopy images, crystal structures, and simulation outputs. Some tasks stay within one program; eight mixed tasks require handoffs between tools. That variety makes the benchmark resemble actual research work more closely than a collection of isolated questions or simplified software demonstrations.

speaker: Noah
line: Quick question: does the benchmark count a task as failed if an agent completes most of the workflow but misses the final save?

speaker: John
line: It records partial progress as well as full completion. Each task has independently checkable criteria, such as opening a file, setting a parameter, exporting an artifact, and saving it in the right place. The normalized score reflects the weighted criteria completed, whereas success rate requires every criterion to pass. This is useful diagnostically: a partial score can reveal progress, while a failed final handoff still signals that the workflow was not completed.

speaker: John
line: The experiments run in a reproducible Windows 11 virtual machine. For graphical tasks, agents see full screenshots and use mouse coordinates, keyboard input, clipboard operations, and window controls; they do not receive accessibility trees in the main evaluation. Code agents instead receive execution feedback. Final states are checked using methods such as file inspection, optical character recognition, pixel analysis, and output parsing, so the scoring connects visible actions to concrete results.

speaker: Noah
line: So you're saying the models can often make progress, but keeping every step correct is the bigger challenge?

speaker: John
line: Exactly. The best overall result, from G-P-T five point four, was a normalized score of 51.2% and a full success rate of 34.3%. Claude reached 33.8% success overall, while the highest average success rate on graphical tasks was 25%. This gap between partial score and full completion suggests that agents can satisfy intermediate requirements but struggle to maintain a correct state across dependent operations.

speaker: John
line: The domain differences are revealing. DigitalMicrograph was particularly difficult, with no model above 20% success, while Materials Studio also challenged agents. Code tasks were easier overall: G-P-T five point four reached 45% success, and its OPTIMADE tasks reached as high as 85%. OriginPro separated models sharply: G-P-T five point four achieved 68.8% success, but several other models rarely completed those combined interface-and-scripting tasks.

speaker: Noah
line: Can you clarify why brief workflow hints make such a noticeable difference?

speaker: John
line: Professional software often contains conventions that are poorly represented in general training data. In ablations, removing hints reduced Doubao's JADE success from 25% to 5%, and its DigitalMicrograph success from 20% to zero. Removing guidance also erased G-P-T five point four's Materials Project successes. In OriginPro, script templates and workflow hints helped agents avoid GUI-only attempts that produced incorrect axes, missing annotations, or no saved output.

speaker: John
line: A practical example is an agent transferring a spectrum from one application to another. It may perform the analysis correctly but export to the wrong path, choose an unusable extension, or save content that the next program cannot read. The mixed tasks expose this boundary problem. They also show why success cannot be judged solely by whether each program appeared to respond: the artifact must remain correct and usable throughout the workflow.

speaker: Noah
line: How does this relate to ScienceBoard and general desktop benchmarks such as O-S-World 2.0?

speaker: John
line: Those benchmarks help establish the broader direction: agents are being tested in longer, more realistic settings, including scientific work and desktop interaction. MatToolBench adds a domain-specific stress test, where legacy interfaces, scientific conventions, APIs, and file handoffs all matter together. The comparisons are informative, not controlled head-to-head experiments, because the tasks, observations, and scoring differ. The contribution is therefore a focused evaluation of challenges that general desktop scores may not capture.

speaker: Noah
line: Hold on, does success here show that an agent's materials analysis is scientifically trustworthy?

speaker: John
line: No, and that limitation is essential. The benchmark checks whether tasks and outputs meet specified criteria; it does not establish that a chosen setting or interpretation is scientifically sound. It also covers ten tools, English instructions, and sessions limited to 50 steps, while some visual checks can vary with rendering. Future work could broaden tool coverage and add workflow memory, tutorial retrieval, API-version awareness, and stronger verification, while keeping human review in the loop.

speaker: John
line: The central takeaway is that scientific agents need more than visual recognition or fluent code generation. They must understand software-specific procedures, verify intermediate states, and preserve artifacts across tools. MatToolBench makes those requirements measurable through realistic tasks and partial-credit diagnostics, while also showing how far current systems remain from dependable end-to-end workflows. Its results offer researchers a map of concrete failure points, not a certificate of scientific correctness. Thanks for listening.
